## Supplementary Figures and Tables {.unnumbered}

::: {#suppfig-depth}
![](figureS1.png)

Control-level HPV detection within matched sequencing-depth bins. For each sample group, the percentage of libraries reaching the control-calibrated detection floor (`r p1(stats$floor_rpm)` RPM) is plotted within five total-read bins (<5M, 5–10M, 10–20M, 20–40M, >40M reads); a group is drawn in a bin only where it has at least three libraries. Productive controls (warts/condyloma) detect at 90–100% in every bin in which they occur, as do the EV biopsies in the deep bins where they fall, whereas cutaneous neoplasia (cSCC/actinic keratosis) and unselected skin stay near zero across all bins, including the deepest. This depth-matched comparison confirms that the group difference in @fig-rpm is not produced by differences in sequencing depth: the groups that reach the floor do so at every depth, and the groups that do not never reach it, however deeply sequenced. Point size is proportional to the number of libraries in each group × bin.
:::

::: {#suppfig-trace}
![](figureS2.png)

What the sub-threshold trace is made of. Every HPV-positive library below the control-calibrated detection floor (`r tr("floor")` RPM) in unselected skin and neoplasia (*n* = `r tr("trace_n")`), set against the productive controls (warts and EV, *n* = `r tr("ctrl_n")`), split into three exclusive classes from the per-gene read counts the pipeline already writes: libraries with no reads on any HPV gene, libraries with gene-mapped reads that do not reach the productive threshold, and productive libraries (L1 ≥ 3 reads). Cell-line and engineered libraries are excluded throughout. The classes are assigned in that order of precedence, so a library appears in exactly one. The residual sample group with no recorded site is not in the denominator: the claim is about skin and neoplasia. Of the `r tr("trace_mid")` gene-mapped but non-productive trace libraries, `r tr("trace_mid_early")` carry early-gene reads with the late programme absent and `r tr("trace_mid_lateonly")` carry only L2 reads below the productive bar; the median late-read fraction across the whole trace is `r trn("trace_medlate")`, against `r trn("ctrl_medlate")` in the controls, which is the differentiation-coupled capsid burst the controls are there to show.
:::

::: {#suppfig-types}
![](figureS3.png)

The HPV type landscape, assigned catalog against detection level. An overview of the two type catalogs tabulated in full in @supptbl-types and @supptbl-trace below, laid out as one grid because the two tables partition a single cohort: a library either clears the assignment criterion (coverage breadth ≥ 0.10 **and** mean depth ≥ 2) and appears in the upper panel, or resolves to a confident type below it and appears in the lower panel, never both. Columns are HPV types grouped by genus and ordered within each genus by total libraries; rows are sample groups, with each group's size on the axis. Fill is the prevalence of that type *within* that group, as a Beta-Binomial posterior mean under a Beta(0.5, 0.5) prior, the same estimator the tables use; the number printed in each cell is the raw library count. Prevalence rather than count is what the color encodes because group sizes span 10 to `r comma(stats$uns_n)` libraries, so counts are not comparable across rows: three libraries is 23% of the EV group and 0.04% of unselected skin. The scale is log~10~ for the same reason, spanning 0.02% to 91%, and gray marks a type not seen in that group at all. Read that way the two panels say different things. The assigned catalog is concentrated in two rows, productive controls and cell lines, and almost entirely in the alpha block, which is the productive-lesion signal and the contamination signal respectively. The unselected-skin row is pale in both panels, and that is the finding rather than an absence: no single cutaneous type is common in healthy skin, but in the detection panel that row runs almost the full width of the beta and gamma blocks, each type carried by a handful of libraries. A commensal reservoir is diverse and individually rare, and it is visible here as the length of that row rather than the intensity of any cell in it. Those same types are largely missing from the assigned panel, because they sit below the coverage threshold a type assignment requires, not because they are absent. @fig-genus collapses both panels from type to genus.
:::

::: {#suppfig-reservoir-gut}
![](figureS4.png)

The DNA reservoir across body sites, the positive control for the composition read-out. Skin (n = `r comma(rvn("n_skin_lib"))` HPV-positive libraries), vaginal (n = `r comma(rvn("n_vaginal_lib"))`) and gut (n = `r comma(rvn("n_gut_lib"))`) metagenomes tabulated from the same catalog by the same code as @fig-reservoir. (**A**) Genus composition of each site's HPV-positive libraries. A library carrying two types of different genera contributes to both, so the panel is normalized within site and shows the composition of type detections rather than prevalence. *Unresolved* is a contig assigned a papillomavirus identity that cannot be placed in a genus, *Novel* a cluster with no reference match. (**B**) The ten most frequent types at each site; the numbers beside the skin bars are that type's assigned / trace detections among the `r comma(rvn("n_skin_rna"))` unselected-skin RNA libraries of this study, as in @fig-reservoir A. This figure is what licenses the skin composition in @fig-reservoir to be read as biology: the identical procedure applied to vaginal libraries recovers an overwhelmingly alpha mucosal niche, which assembly noise could not produce. Only skin is carried into the main figure, since the paper's subject is skin. Its composition is a mixture of mucosal alpha (`r p1(rvn("gut_alpha"))`%) and cutaneous beta (`r p1(rvn("gut_beta"))`%), and its commonest types interleave the two (HPV16, HPV6 and HPV56 with HPV24, HPV124 and HPV37), which is the expected signature of a collection route that crosses perianal skin rather than of papillomavirus carriage in the gut; the same pattern is seen independently in rectal-swab cohorts. Read that way the site is a useful control, since it shows the catalog recovering the genus of whatever epithelium the sampling route touches, and its novel-cluster fraction (`r p1(rvn("gut_novel_any"))`%) sits with skin's (`r p1(rvn("skin_novel_any"))`%) rather than with the vaginal site's (`r p1(rvn("vaginal_novel_any"))`%), as expected if its beta/gamma content is cutaneous in origin.
:::

::: {#suppfig-bayes}
![](figureS5.png)

The Bayesian re-analysis as a forest plot. The same posterior summaries tabulated in @supptbl-bayes, drawn on a log odds-ratio axis: each point is the posterior median odds ratio and the bar through it the 95% credible interval, with the dashed line at OR = 1 marking no effect. Filled points mark intervals that exclude 1; the two open grey points are the intervals that do not, and both are sequencing-depth terms, so the figure shows directly that deeper sequencing buys no productive-level detection either across sample groups or within neoplasia. P(OR > 1) is the posterior probability of a positive effect, on the same rounding as the text. Contrast labels and their order are those of @supptbl-bayes; the Student-*t*(3) row is the prior-sensitivity refit of the contrast immediately above it, reported in that table's caption rather than as a row of its own, and it sits further from 1 rather than nearer, which is what makes the productive-controls gap a finding rather than an artifact of the Normal prior. The axis spans five orders of magnitude because that contrast genuinely does.
:::

::: {#supptbl-types}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat(knitr::kable(build_type_table(), format = "pipe", align = c("l", rep("r", 6))), sep = "\n")
```

Number of libraries assigned to each HPV reference type across sample groups (types with ≥2 assigned libraries shown). @suppfig-types shows this catalog and that of @supptbl-trace together as a single grid. Each cell also gives, in parentheses, the prevalence *within* that group, the library count divided by the group size in the column header, estimated as a Beta-Binomial posterior mean under a weakly-informative Beta(0.5, 0.5) prior. Because group sizes span more than two orders of magnitude, raw counts are not comparable across groups: the 14 HPV11 detections in productive controls represent a far higher prevalence than the 24 HPV16 detections in the much larger cell-line group (`r ciA("HPV11","control_productive")` versus `r ciA("HPV16","cell_line")`; posterior mean with 95% credible interval), and the high-risk mucosal types HPV16 and HPV18 are confined almost entirely to cell-line material (`r ciA("HPV16","cell_line")` and `r ciA("HPV18","cell_line")` of cell-line libraries, versus below 0.1% of skin libraries for both), the signature of integrated-HPV cell-line contamination. Productive controls are dominated by cutaneous wart and low-risk types (HPV57, HPV2, HPV27, HPV6/11, HPV42); the EV group by the beta-types that define the syndrome (HPV9, HPV14, HPV20, HPV25, HPV47). The neoplasia-associated infections are the beta- and alpha-types HPV12, HPV16, HPV96 and HPV182. Unselected skin contributes no type above the two-library display threshold apart from two HPV18 contamination calls: its beta/gamma reservoir lies below the breadth-and-depth assignment criterion and appears instead in @supptbl-trace. @fig-genus summarizes this table, and @supptbl-trace, at the level of HPV genus.
:::

::: {#supptbl-productive}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat(knitr::kable(build_prod_table(), format = "pipe", align = c("l", "l", "l", "r", "r", "r")), sep = "\n")
```

Genuine, non-cell-line productive HPV infections detected in primary skin and skin-associated tissue. Each library met the productive criterion (≥3 L1 major-capsid reads) and was flagged as primary tissue rather than cell line or engineered material. Coverage breadth is the maximum across assigned references for that sample. In the two site-unrecorded co-infections (ERR2274877, ERR1971044, both from cutaneous actinic-keratosis/cSCC cohorts) the co-infecting beta-type HPV182 reached 98–99% genome coverage at 243–245× mean depth. These cases show that bona fide productive cutaneous beta- and gamma-HPV infection does occur in primary tissue, but against the population-scale null they are the exception (see main text and @fig-rpm).
:::

::: {#supptbl-bayes}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat(knitr::kable(build_bayes_table(stats, bget), format = "pipe", align = c("l", "l", "l", "r")), sep = "\n")
```

Bayesian re-analysis of the principal contrasts under weakly-informative priors. Each frequentist model (M1–M3; Methods, @tbl-positivity, @fig-rpm) was refitted as a Bayesian logistic regression with a Normal(0, 2.5) prior on the log-odds coefficients and a Normal(0, 5) prior on the intercept (`rstanarm`; four chains, all R-hat ≤ 1.004, no divergent transitions). Odds ratios are posterior medians with 95% credible intervals; P(OR > 1) is the posterior probability of a positive effect. Frequentist odds ratios (with *P* values) are shown for comparison; the productive-controls-versus-skin row is a Fisher exact estimate inflated by near-complete separation, whose Bayesian counterpart is regularized by the prior (a heavier-tailed Student-*t*(3) prior gives an even larger posterior OR, `r bor(bget("M2c_controls_vs_skin_floor_studentt"))`, confirming robustness). Sequencing depth is modeled per 10-fold (log₁₀) change in library size.
:::

::: {#supptbl-cin}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat(knitr::kable(cin_tbl, format = "pipe", align = c("l", "l", "l", "l", "l", "r")), sep = "\n")
```

High-risk mucosal HPV16 cases captured by the broadened cutaneous-neoplasia query and conservatively retained in the neoplasia group. All `r stats$cin_n` are typed as the mucosal high-risk type HPV16 (dominant assigned reference) while carrying squamous-cell-carcinoma diagnoses at a cutaneous or unrecorded site, and all exceed the control-calibrated detection floor (`r p1(stats$floor_rpm)` RPM), so they make up `r stats$cin_n` of the `r stats$neo_pos_floor` above-floor detections in the whole group. Excluding them halves cutaneous-neoplasia floor-level detection, from `r pp(stats$neo_pctfloor)`% to `r pp(stats$neo_pctfloor_cut)`% (versus unselected skin: OR `r fo(stats$m2b_or_cut)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m2b_p_cut)`, down from OR `r fo(stats$m2b_or)`), and strengthens the warts/EV-versus-neoplasia productivity contrast from OR `r fo(stats$m3_or)` to OR `r fo(stats$m3_or_cut)` (*P* = `r fp(stats$m3_p_cut)`). Retaining them is therefore the conservative analytical choice: the small floor-level excess of neoplasia over skin reported in the main text is an upper bound. Virus–host junction calling supports the same reading from an independent direction: the members of this set that carry enough viral reads to test are integration-positive, whereas the cutaneous-neoplasia libraries outside it are not. Integration is the expected state of mucosal HPV16 in carcinoma and is not a property of the cutaneous reservoir, so the assignment of these libraries to a mucosal origin rests on genome state as well as on type.
:::

::: {#supptbl-chem}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
if (nrow(chem_tbl)) cat(knitr::kable(chem_tbl, format = "pipe", align = c("l", rep("r", 6))), sep = "\n")
```

Library-selection chemistry by sample group, as a percentage of the libraries in each group (group size in parentheses). Chemistry was called from SRA `LibrarySelection` where that field carries a specific value, and otherwise from the free-text library-construction protocol (Methods); `r pp(stats$chem_pct)`% of the `r comma(stats$chem_total)` libraries resolved, the remainder being records in which neither source states how the library was selected. The table exists because poly-A capture is the chemistry least favorable to viral-transcript recovery, so an unbalanced distribution of chemistry across groups could in principle manufacture the productivity contrast reported in the main text. It does not: the imbalance runs the other way. The neoplasia group, in which no productive infection is found, is rRNA-depleted in `r pp(stats$chem_neo_ribo)`% of libraries against `r pp(stats$chem_skin_ribo)`% of unselected skin, while the productive controls, in which productive infection is abundant, contain no rRNA-depleted libraries at all. The two selection chemistries are in any case indistinguishable in their yield of trace HPV reads once depth and group are accounted for (rRNA-depleted versus poly-A, OR `r fo(stats$chem_ribo_or)`, 95% CI `r oci(stats$chem_ribo_lo, stats$chem_ribo_hi)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$chem_ribo_p)`); the levels that do carry more trace signal are the amplification chemistries, template-switching (OR `r fo(stats$chem_smart_or)`) and 3'-barcoded droplet libraries (OR `r fo(stats$chem_tenx_or)`), which is the profile of amplification and barcode-swapping artifact rather than of recovery. Restricting the skin-versus-neoplasia contrast to the `r comma(stats$ribo_n)` rRNA-depleted libraries alone leaves the trace excess intact (OR `r fo(stats$ribo_or)`, `r oci(stats$ribo_lo, stats$ribo_hi)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$ribo_p)`) and yields no above-floor library in either group.
:::

::: {#supptbl-trace}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat(knitr::kable(build_trace_table(), format = "pipe", align = c("l","l","r","r","r","r","r","r")), sep = "\n")
```

Detection-level HPV type catalog, shown alongside @supptbl-types as a grid in @suppfig-types. This table is the complement of @supptbl-types, not an extension of it: it contains only the `r stats$trace_n` HPV-positive libraries that fell *below* the breadth ≥ 0.10 and depth ≥ 2 assignment threshold and therefore have no entry in @supptbl-types. A library appears in exactly one of the two tables. That is why groups dominated by high-coverage infection are nearly empty here: of the `r stats$ctrl_n` productive-control libraries, `r stats$ctrl_n - trace_elig("control_productive")` are assigned a type in @supptbl-types and only `r trace_elig("control_productive")` remain eligible for this table, of which `r stats$trace_ctrl_resolved` resolve. The near-absence of productive controls from the detection level is a positive control on the assignment criterion, not a missing signal. For each eligible library the best-hit reference was taken from unique STAR primary alignments (MAPQ 255); `r stats$trace_resolved` resolved to a confident low-coverage type spanning `r stats$trace_ntypes` types (those with ≥ 2 resolved calls shown), with genus from the complete PaVE lookup. These are low-coverage, non-productive detections: the type is confidently identified but genome coverage is below the assignment breadth, so they extend the descriptive type catalog without bearing on productivity. As in @supptbl-types, each cell gives the count with its prevalence among *all* libraries of that group in parentheses (Beta-Binomial posterior mean, Beta(0.5, 0.5) prior; group sizes in the headers), keeping both tables on one denominator; the trace-eligible counts per group are `r trace_elig_str()`. Healthy skin is dominated by cutaneous beta/gamma/nu types (`r stats$trace_skin_cut` of `r stats$trace_skin_n` resolved skin calls), whereas the mucosal types HPV16 and HPV18 concentrate in cell-line and other material (HPV16 trace prevalence `r ciT("HPV16","cell_line")` in cell lines versus `r ciT("HPV16","unselected_skin")` in skin), reproducing the contamination pattern of @supptbl-types at the sensitivity floor. @fig-genus collapses this table, and @supptbl-types, from HPV type to HPV genus.
:::


::: {#supptbl-coinf}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat(knitr::kable(build_coinf_table(), format = "pipe", align = c("l", "l", "l", "l")), sep = "\n")
```

Libraries carrying more than one assigned HPV type. Every library in which two or more references independently cleared the assignment criterion (coverage breadth ≥ 0.10 **and** mean depth ≥ 2) is listed, with each type's breadth and mean depth, ordered by depth; `r cf$libs` of the `r cf$typed` typed libraries qualify (`r cf$k2` with two types, `r cf$k3` with three, `r cf$k4` with four, `r cf$k5` with five). Coverage is computed by `samtools coverage -q 10`, which retains only uniquely-mapped reads, since STAR assigns MAPQ ≤ 3 to any read placing equally well on two references, so cross-mapping between similar types cannot manufacture a co-infection call: each type in a row is supported by reads that map to it and to nothing else. Three cautions govern how far the table can be read. First, the rows are not independent observations: `r cf$pair_libs` of the `r cf$libs` come from the paired studies SRP314958 (RNA-seq) and SRP314961 (MeRIP-seq), which are condyloma lesions from `r cf$pair_donors` donors (CA_1 to CA_5), each sequenced as an RNA-seq library plus a MeRIP input and IP fraction, so rows sharing a donor carry near-identical read profiles. Second, the secondary types often sit close to the threshold: across all non-dominant calls the median depth is `r p1(cf$sec_med_depth)`× and `r cf$sec_shallow`% fall below 5×, so which type is called second can depend on the library fraction, and in donor CA_2 the RNA-seq and MeRIP input fractions call HPV6 + HPV11 while the IP fraction of the same specimen calls HPV6 + HPV42. Third, the deepest type in a co-infected library typically dominates its partner, by a median of `r fo(cf$dom_ratio_med)`-fold (interquartile range `r fo(cf$dom_ratio_lo)` to `r fo(cf$dom_ratio_hi)`), so most rows describe one established infection alongside a minor second type rather than two comparable ones. Where both partners are unambiguous the pairings are biologically coherent: two carcinoma and actinic-keratosis libraries whose SRA records carry no tissue field (ERR2274877, ERR1971044) carry the beta-types HPV96 and HPV182 together at 98–99% breadth and 61–245× depth, and an EV biopsy (SRR21205038) carries the beta-types HPV20 and HPV9 at 18,558× and 736×; both are two full genomes in one library, not a genome plus a fragment. The most frequent pairing in the study is HPV11 with HPV42: `r cf$both1142` libraries carry both, against `r cf$only11` with HPV11 alone and `r cf$only42` with HPV42 alone. Requiring both partners to clear a stricter bar (breadth ≥ 0.70 and depth ≥ 5× for each) leaves `r cf$strict_libs` libraries from `r cf$strict_donors` of those donors (CA_1). Their dominance relation is asymmetric: HPV11 is the deeper type in all five condyloma lesions, exceeding HPV42 48- to 4,100-fold in the three with a strong HPV11 signal (CA_1, CA_4, CA_5) and 2- to 4-fold in the other two, so HPV42 is the minor partner throughout and clears the assignment threshold only where it happens to be abundant. Whether the pairing is a genuine dual infection or an artifact of that sensitivity limit cannot be settled from five donors of one study: it is a hypothesis the data motivate, not a result they support.
:::

## Above-floor HPV in tissue that cannot host it: two contaminated studies {#sec-s-crosstalk}

The non-permissive tissue group is defined by biology, not by its HPV content, so
it also exposes the opposite case: libraries from non-permissive material that
carry HPV *above* the trace level. Two studies do, and both were held out of the
control group for that reason.

SRP572742 (skeletal muscle and blood from myotonic dystrophy patients,
*n* = 66) is HPV-positive at any level in 83% of libraries, with 3 crossing the
control-calibrated detection floor and a maximum of 5.3 RPM. Neither muscle nor
blood contains stratified squamous epithelium, so no part of that signal can be
infection of the sampled tissue.

SRP565659 makes the point under internal control. It is a multi-omic
cutaneous T-cell lymphoma study in which skin and peripheral blood were taken
from the same patients and sequenced together (Table S1 of the source
publication assigns every run a tissue). Its 26 skin libraries are strongly
HPV-positive, 88% at any level and up to 12.0 RPM, as expected for lesional
skin. Its 42 blood and lymph-node libraries (same patients, same runs, tissue
that cannot host the virus) are HPV-positive at 52%, up to 3.6 RPM, with one
library above the floor.

The pattern in both is a minority of reads appearing in libraries with no
biological source for them, alongside co-sequenced libraries carrying a genuine
high-titre signal. That is the signature of index hopping and inter-library
carry-over rather than infection, and it is the same phenomenon that makes
cell-line contamination the dominant driver of apparent HPV positivity in public
transcriptomes. Two consequences follow for how the trace signal should be read. First,
a non-zero HPV read count in a single library is not evidence of infection even
when the tissue is plausible, which is why the analysis here is anchored on a
control-calibrated floor rather than on detection. Second, studies whose design
places high-titre and HPV-free material in the same sequencing run will inflate
apparent prevalence in the HPV-free arm, so prevalence estimates drawn from
public data without a non-permissive control are upper bounds.

::: {#supptbl-e2}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat(knitr::kable(build_e2_table(), format = "pipe",
                 align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r")), sep = "\n")
```

E2 integrity in assembled papillomavirus contigs, and why it cannot detect integration. Contigs recovered from the Logan-wide papillomavirus catalog [@shenpv2026] were annotated by `tblastn` against RefSeq papillomavirus open reading frames, and scored for whether E2 is present given that E1 is present. The comparison that matters is between the two right-hand columns and the two left-hand ones. Across all contigs, E2 recovery tracks assembly quality rather than biology: it is lowest in cervical CIN (79.3%) and cervical carcinoma (83.6%), which are also the arms with the shortest contigs, and highest in the vaginal and gut metagenomes, which assemble best. Once the question is restricted to near-complete contigs (≥7 kb), where E2 presence can actually be assessed, every category converges on 100%, and cervical carcinoma, in which integration and E2 disruption are the rule, returns 99.3% against 99.9% for skin. That convergence is not a biological result. An integrated genome cannot assemble across the virus-host junction, so conditioning on completeness selects episomal genomes in every category, and the statistic is structurally incapable of detecting the event it was built to detect. This table is reported because the inference is an inviting one to draw from a public contig catalog, and because it bounds what the DNA axis can contribute: presence of a papillomavirus in such a catalog is presence of a detectable L1, and carries no information about the state of the genome (Discussion).
:::
